\title{When Modal Contact Rows Fail in Fixed-Budget XPBD:\\
  Diagnosis and an Operating Guide}

\author{Anonymous Author(s)}

\begin{abstract}
Rigid-body XPBD engines already resolve contacts and joints, and adding a small
global modal state ($16$--$24$ amplitudes) is an attractive way to give a stiff
prop low-cost vibration without converting it into a full nodal/tet deformable.
We show that inserting this globally shared modal state directly into a two-way
unilateral contact row is not automatically energy-safe when the host runs only
a few local iterations per substep. Across three scenes, two relaxations and
four schedules, \emph{our tested XPBD implementation} overdraws the measured
gross rigid-side supply by up to $4.4\times10^{7}$~J (a $2.2$--$4.5\times10^{7}$~J
neighborhood over a deterministic perturbation ensemble), while
augmented-Lagrangian and implicit implementations are markedly milder controls
($\le6.7$~J in $3$ of $24$ cells and never, respectively; a gravity/no-contact
accounting audit places the control floor below $10^{-3}$~J, so $6.7$~J is real
injection). A same-path iteration ladder, equal-row-count schedules,
warm-starting and mode truncation localize this catastrophic amplification
to finite-budget convergence of the shared modal coupling, and an in-host
block-condensation ablation shows condensing the shared rows does \emph{not} fix
it. When the contact architecture is flexible the tested stiffness-aware
implicit realization is the preferred observed control; in a fixed XPBD host,
spend the local budget on iterations and verify the modal basis --- more
substeps and a block solve do not suffice. For hosts that still cannot converge,
a cumulative modal-storage projection enforces its scalar accounting bound
unconditionally (Prop.~\ref{prop:guarantee}, roundoff floor in all $90$ measured
cells) but opens up to $21.6$~mm of penetration ($72\%$ of the board's
thickness), and is therefore containment, not corrected contact.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% =====================================================================
A developer building an interactive scene on a rigid-body XPBD
engine~\citep{macklin2016xpbd} already has a solver that resolves contacts and
joints under a small, fixed local-iteration budget. To make a stiff prop ---
a shelf, a table, a ledge --- ring when it is struck, the tempting move is not
to replace it with a full nodal or tetrahedral deformable, which adds thousands
of online coordinates and local internal constraints, but to attach a small
precomputed modal basis: $16$--$24$ global amplitudes $\mathbf{q}$ capturing the
low-frequency bending of a stiff, small-displacement
body~\citep{james2002dyrt,hauser2003,peng2024reduced}. The runtime state grows
by a handful of numbers, the precomputation is offline, and the same XPBD host
steps everything. This paper is written for that developer, not to argue XPBD
against another solver.

The catch is in the contact. A modal prop driven \emph{one way} --- an external
filter reads detected contact events and rings the modes with no back-reaction
--- is the real-time precedent~\citep{coevoet2020distant}, but it double-counts
the interface energy and cannot let the prop's own deformation change how it is
supported. The physically consistent move is a \emph{two-way} row: rigid and
modal unknowns resolved together through one shared contact
multiplier~\citep{zheng2011}, so a heavier load bends the support and the bent
support redistributes the load. The trap is that every support contact touches
the \emph{same} global vector $\mathbf{q}$, so the contact-row graph is dense on
the modes even though the state is tiny --- and a host running only a few local
iterations per substep need not converge that shared coupling. We take the row as
given: at position level it is one linearization step from the velocity-level
law ($C^{n+1}\!\approx\!C^{n}+h\,\mathbf{J}\mathbf{u}^{n+1}$, same Jacobian and
multiplier as~\citet{zheng2011}), narrower than the original --- normal rows
only, $e{=}0$ restitution --- and \emph{not} a contribution of this paper. Our
question is the practitioner's: what does the obvious two-way transcription cost
at a normal budget, and what should one do about it? \emph{If solver architecture
is unconstrained our evidence favors the tested stiffness-aware velocity-level
realization; our target is the existing fixed-budget XPBD host.}

Finite-iteration coupling across a partition boundary can inject spurious energy
even when every subsystem is individually passive~\citep{wei2026earlyterm}, and
velocity-level frictional contact spanning rigid and reduced deformable bodies,
with the energy artifacts of iterative solvers named, goes back at least
to~\citet{kaufman2008}. What is missing, and what we supply, is a quantitative
account of this case --- unilateral contact-to-modal transfer in a fixed-budget
host --- and an operating guide for the practitioner who hits it.

\paragraph*{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A practitioner workflow and its failure.} We treat adding a compact
  modal state to a fixed-budget XPBD host as the workflow it is, and show that the
  direct two-way contact row overdraws its measured rigid-side supply
  catastrophically at interactive budgets --- across three scenes, two relaxations
  and four schedules (\S\ref{sec:matrix}) --- with augmented-Lagrangian and
  implicit implementations as milder controls. The cross-control reading is
  secured by a gravity/no-contact accounting audit and the failure's robustness by
  a deterministic perturbation ensemble.
\item \textbf{Mechanism and an operating guide.} A same-path iteration ladder,
  equal-row-count schedules, warm-starting, mode truncation and an in-host
  block-condensation ablation localize the amplification to finite-budget
  convergence of the shared modal coupling (\S\ref{sec:kconv}), and yield an
  ordered decision rule: the tested implicit realization when the architecture is
  flexible, otherwise iterations and a verified basis --- not more substeps, not a
  block solve --- in a fixed XPBD host.
\item \textbf{A last-resort guardrail, priced.} A cumulative modal-storage bound
  funded by the measured rigid-side loss and enforced by a scalar projection of
  the realized state (\S\ref{sec:bound}): a deliberately minimal fail-safe, not a
  contact method, guaranteed unconditionally (Prop.~\ref{prop:guarantee}, roundoff
  floor in all $90$ measured cells) but at a measured cost to contact validity
  (\S\ref{sec:validity}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph*{Related work.} Rigid XPBD~\citep{macklin2016xpbd}, interactive modal
deformation and velocity-level modal contact~\citep{james2002dyrt,hauser2003,%
zheng2011,kaufman2008}, and reduced XPBD~\citep{peng2024reduced} set the stage;
the last uses modes as a \emph{deformation} surrogate, whereas here modal
amplitudes enter as contact DOFs driven by the shared multiplier
(cf.~ray-traced penalty contact without a shared unilateral
multiplier~\citep{zobel2025unity}). Our last-resort guardrail transplants
energy-tank control~\citep{hannaford2002,franken2011,rath2008} rather than
inventing one: we keep the tank-and-observer structure but fund the tank from
\emph{measured} rigid-side loss --- not the port it regulates --- and scale
realized \emph{state} rather than a force, because a fixed-budget solver commits
its multipliers before the excess is observable. This separates it from
total-energy projection~\citep{dinev2018fepr}, bidirectional total-energy
tracking~\citep{you2026energy}, and the structural finite-budget passivity of
\emph{bilateral} couplings~\citep{wei2026earlyterm}.

% =====================================================================
\section{The row and the invariant it must respect}
\label{sec:row}
% =====================================================================
Let $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$ be mass-normalized modal amplitudes of the
supporting body, so its modal mechanical energy is
$\Emod=\tfrac12\dot{\mathbf{q}}^{\!\top}\dot{\mathbf{q}}
      +\tfrac12\mathbf{q}^{\!\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{q}$.
A support-contact row between a rigid corner at world height $y_c$ and the
deformed surface has gap
\begin{equation}
C \;=\; y_c \;-\; \bigl(y_{\mathrm{rest}} + \mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}\bigr),
\qquad C \ge 0,\; \lambda \ge 0,\; C\lambda = 0,
\label{eq:row}
\end{equation}
with $\partial C/\partial\mathbf{q}=-\mathbf{U}_y$, so one multiplier $\lambda$
drives both the rigid body and the modal amplitudes. Equation~\eqref{eq:row} is
the transcription discussed above, not a new law. It is one row \emph{law},
instantiated at every support contact every substep --- $48$ such rows on the
shelf, $40$ on the ledge, $200$ on the table --- all sharing the one modal
state $\mathbf{q}$.

\paragraph*{The invariant.} We require that the energy \emph{stored in the
modal subsystem} never exceed the \emph{measured gross rigid-side loss} ---
defined exactly at \eqref{eq:derig} below --- cumulatively over the run:
\begin{equation}
\Emod^{\,n} - \Emod^{\,0}
\;\;\le\;\;
\eta \sum_{k\le n} \max\!\bigl(\dErig^{\,k},\,0\bigr),
\qquad \eta\in(0,1].
\label{eq:invariant}
\end{equation}
The transfer efficiency $\eta$ sets how much of the measured loss may be spent;
\emph{every experiment in this paper runs $\eta=1$}, the least restrictive
admissible value, so no result below depends on tuning it. The bound is
\emph{cumulative}, not per-step: a substep may deposit more than it earns
provided the running total remains within the budget, which is what lets a
legitimate ring persist across substeps.

\paragraph*{Definitions.} Modal storage is the mechanical energy of the
reduced state as written above, and $\Emod^{\,0}=0$: every scene starts from an
undeformed, resting support, so even the run's own settling transient must be
funded by the reservoir. The supply is
\begin{equation}
\dErig^{\,k} \;=\; \bigl(E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{k,-} - E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{k,+}\bigr)
                 \;+\; W_g^{\,k},
\qquad
W_g^{\,k}=\sum_b m_b\,\mathbf{g}\!\cdot\!\bigl(\mathbf{x}_b^{k,+}-\mathbf{x}_b^{k,-}\bigr),
\label{eq:derig}
\end{equation}
where $E_{\mathrm{rig}}=\sum_b\bigl[\tfrac12 m_b\|\mathbf{v}_b\|^2
+\tfrac12\boldsymbol{\omega}_b^{\!\top}\mathbf{I}_b\boldsymbol{\omega}_b\bigr]$
is \emph{purely kinetic} --- translational and rotational, over all dynamic
bodies, not merely those in contact --- and $\pm$ denote the two ends of substep
$k$. We call this the \textbf{measured gross rigid-side loss}: the scene-wide,
gravity-corrected, gross kinetic-energy loss of the rigid subsystem. It is a
\emph{loss}, not a dissipation --- it also counts legitimate rigid-to-modal
transfer and losses at rigid--rigid contacts elsewhere in the scene --- so it is
an envelope on what contact dissipated, not a measurement of it
(\S\ref{sec:limits}). Gravity enters only through $W_g$, so free ballistic
motion registers zero supply --- a falling body's kinetic gain exactly equals
the gravity work, and only an inelastic velocity change funds the reservoir.
Substep-boundary endpoints tile the timeline exactly, so no rigid energy change
escapes the accounting.

\paragraph*{What the invariant is, and two diagnostics.} The bound
\eqref{eq:invariant} is a cumulative storage ceiling on the modal subsystem
whose supply is \emph{measured, not prescribed} --- the right-hand side is the
measured loss of \eqref{eq:derig}, never a tuned constant or a fraction of
incident energy. It constrains a scalar reservoir, not a contact port, so it is
neither port passivity nor a signed per-interface bound. The \emph{gross} sum
ignores substeps in which the rigid subsystem \emph{gains} energy, and counts
energy returned and re-dissipated as fresh supply (\S\ref{sec:limits} measures
both). We read two diagnostics against the sweep below and keep them distinct:
the incident-energy ratio $R=$~peak modal energy / peak incident rigid KE, a
severity measure, and the signed margin of \eqref{eq:invariant} itself in
joules, the invariant proper; they need not flag the same cells. Enforcing the
bound needs a projection, deferred to \S\ref{sec:bound}.

% =====================================================================
\section{The failure at a fixed budget}
% =====================================================================
All solver-behaviour measurements below come from a single machine (Apple M4,
CPU, CPython 3.12); every number is frozen with its generating command and
commit hash in the supplemental ledger. We deliberately avoid mixing
machines: chaotic contact stacks diverge across architectures under
floating-point reassociation.

\subsection{One row, three implementations, the same 24 cells}
\label{sec:matrix}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.86\textwidth]{fig_xpbd_map.pdf}
\caption{Our tested XPBD implementation, over the 24-cell sweep (3 scenes
$\times$ relaxation $\{0.7,1.0\}$ $\times$ budget), governor OFF. \textbf{Left,
top:} $R$ = peak modal energy / peak incident rigid KE, a severity diagnostic;
\textbf{bottom:} the signed margin of \eqref{eq:invariant} in joules ($>0$
violates). The two disagree by design (XPBD: $R{>}1$ in $8/24$, margin$>0$ in
$9/24$) --- a result, not noise. \textbf{Right:} a compact control strip for the
three implementations (one of each, \emph{not} compliance- or cost-matched):
violating cells, worst margin, worst $R$. This is a scale gap, not a ranking ---
$4.4\times10^{7}$~J vs.\ $\le6.7$~J vs.\ $0$; the E1 accounting audit puts the
control floor below $10^{-3}$~J, so $6.7$~J is real injection. The full
two-metric 72-cell three-implementation heatmap is in the supplement.}
\label{fig:matrix}
\end{figure*}

We drive an impactor into a modally reduced support in three scenes --- a shelf
board, a ledge slab, and a $2.2\times1.1$~m table, the last two following the
layouts of \citet{coevoet2020distant} --- and sweep modal relaxation and the
local budget (iterations $\times$ substeps) over
$\{4{\times}1, 8{\times}2, 16{\times}4, 32{\times}8\}$. The hosts are
XPBD~\citep{macklin2016xpbd}, AVBD~\citep{giles2025avbd} (a descendant of vertex
block descent~\citep{chen2024vbd}), and a sequential-impulse realization in the
sense of~\citet{catto2005iterative}, made implicit in the modal block. All three
are pinned to $h{=}1/120$~s, per-substep contact regeneration, modal rank
$16/16/24$ (shelf/ledge/table), Rayleigh damping, an \emph{implicit-midpoint}
modal restoring step, and $\eta{=}1$; they differ in the unknown solved for
(position / position\,+\,multiplier / velocity), the modal contact weight ---
XPBD's explicit per-mode compliance $1/(H_{ii}h^2{-}1)$ versus the impulse host's
implicit $(\mathbf{M}{+}h\mathbf{D}{+}h^2\mathbf{K})^{-1}$ --- warm start, and
relaxation (the full host/parameter table is in the supplement). Two differences
matter. Relaxation is \emph{inert} on the impulse host (its implicit modal weight
needs no under-relaxation), so its two relaxation rows are bit-identical. Warm
start also differs ($\lambda\!\leftarrow\!0$ every substep for the position-based
host, carried duals for the others), so the comparison is as-deployed, not
compliance-matched --- but it is not the lever: warm-starting the position-based
host leaves the footprint unchanged (the same $8/24$ cells, worst
$1.20\times10^{5}$) and \emph{worse} at $4{\times}1$ ($3.1\times$), a warm
multiplier being unable to converge the shared modal DOF that only iterations do
(\S\ref{sec:kconv}).

\paragraph*{Equal row evaluations, unequal outcome.} A cell costs $K\!\cdot\!S$
row evaluations per frame, so the budget axis spans $\times64$ and conflates two
refinements that are neither interchangeable nor equally priced (a substep also
repeats contact generation and integration). At $32$ row evaluations on the
shelf drop, spent as iterations ($K{=}32,S{=}1$) the ratio is $0.300$ and
\eqref{eq:invariant} holds; spent as substeps ($K{=}4,S{=}8$) it is $3.13$,
overdrawing by $481$~J: substep refinement alone does not converge the row.

Figure~\ref{fig:matrix} shows the outcome. The position-based host exceeds
$R=1$ in $8$ of $24$ cells, worst case $1.19534\times10^{5}$ (ledge, relaxation
$1.0$, $4{\times}1$: peak modal energy $4.44\times10^{7}$~J against an incident
$371$~J); the augmented-Lagrangian host in $2$ of $24$ --- both at the starved
$4{\times}1$ corner of the table scene, worst $1.70$ --- so it is not
unconditionally benign either. The ordering is scene-dependent and it inverts:
worst-over-scenes at $4{\times}1$ the position-based host is five orders of
magnitude more energetic in the ratio $R$ ($1.2\times10^{5}$ vs $1.70$), yet on the table scene
itself the augmented-Lagrangian host is the worse ($1.18$ and $1.70$ against a
position-based worst of $0.37$). Neither host dominates across scenes.

\paragraph*{The ratio is not the invariant.} We also measure
\eqref{eq:invariant} directly on all three hosts, ungoverned, running the
reservoir accounting live while forcing $\gamma\equiv1$: every state write in the
enforcement path is guarded by $\gamma<1$, so the trajectory is bit-identical to
an ungoverned run (the ratios above reproduce the independent sweep exactly). The
two diagnostics do not flag the same cells --- the position-based host violates
\eqref{eq:invariant} in $9$ of $24$ against $R>1$ in $8$, the augmented-Lagrangian
host in $3$ against $2$, the implicit host in neither ($0/24$, worst margin at
the roundoff floor) --- so neither subsumes the other. What orders the failures
is magnitude: the position-based overdraw reaches $4.4\times10^{7}$~J, seven
orders past the largest augmented-Lagrangian one ($6.7$~J, at the starved
$4{\times}1$ table corner) and past the implicit host's exact zero. A
gravity/no-contact accounting audit puts that control floor below $10^{-3}$~J on
both non-injecting hosts --- three to four orders under $6.7$~J --- so the
augmented-Lagrangian overdraft is real impact-driven injection, not accounting
noise: three regimes the ratio-to-incident-energy diagnostic compresses into one
number.


\subsection{The position-based amplification is a truncation artifact}
\label{sec:kconv}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{fig_operating_envelope.pdf}
\caption{The XPBD operating envelope (our tested position-based host, governor
OFF). \textbf{(a)}~Injection $R$ vs.\ local iterations $K$ on a deterministic
shelf drop ($S{=}1$): $R$ decays monotonically toward the implicit reference
($0.273$), crossing the incident-energy threshold between $K{=}16$ and $24$.
Annotated: the $32{\times}1$-vs-$4{\times}8$ equal-row pair (same $32$ row
evaluations, but spent as substeps it still injects) and warm-starting (no help;
worse at $4{\times}1$). \textbf{(b)}~The end-of-substep gap converges with $K$,
confirming the falling ratio is the \emph{row} converging, not a scalar
shrinking coincidentally. \textbf{(c)}~Shared-row treatment (E6a-1): serial
per-row support projection (the paper path) vs.\ joint block condensation, both
scenes. The serial path converges/holds by $16{\times}4$--$32{\times}1$; block
condensation does \emph{not} --- a different, worse convergence path that injects
where serial holds. Condensing the shared rows is not the fix.}
\label{fig:kconv}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:kconv} isolates the local iteration budget. Two references
recur below and are not the same object: \emph{the implicit reference} is the
implicit high-iteration realization at $K{=}500$ --- the same code path run to
$K{=}500$ --- and \emph{the XPBD self-reference} is the position-based host run
to $K{=}500$ against itself. The position-based
host falls monotonically from $2.96\times10^{4}$ at $K{=}1$ to $0.300$ at
$K{=}32$, approaching the implicit reference $0.2735$; the gap
$|\text{XPBD}-\text{reference}|$ shrinks from $2.96\times10^{4}$ to
$2.7\times10^{-2}$. The implicit realization moves only in the fourth decimal
across $K=2\ldots500$ (max$-$min $6.8\times10^{-4}$).

A falling energy ratio does not by itself show that the \emph{row} is
converging --- a single scalar could shrink coincidentally. Measuring the
constraint directly resolves the question, and the two complementarity
conditions must be read in their own units rather than compounded into one
dimensionally mixed scalar. End-of-substep penetration falls from $27.9$~mm at
$K{=}1$ to $3.6\,\mu$m by $K{=}64$, where it saturates. The multiplier
surviving on \emph{separated} rows --- force where the gap is open, in units of
the steady-state median --- instead \emph{rises} from $84\times$ to $139\times$
through $K{=}24$, collapsing to exactly zero only at $K{=}64$. The energy
crossing at $K\approx24$ therefore coincides with the \emph{gap} converging,
not with complementarity holding: the multiplier side clears a rung later.
Position-based host only --- the augmented-Lagrangian multiplier is not the
same object, and the implicit realization is converged at $K{=}2$.

\paragraph*{Self-convergence stops short of the reference.} Running the
position-based host to $K\!=\!500$ against itself does not close the gap: its
ratio plateaus by $K\approx64$ at $0.2996$, so the residual $2.6\times10^{-2}$
against the reference's $0.2735$ is a fixed point, not a tail. The state agrees
no better --- on the deflection trajectory
$d_i(t)=\mathbf{U}_y[i]^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}(t)$ the peak matches to $2.4\%$ but
the trajectories differ by $6.8$~mm, $34\%$ of the reference's own peak. The two
hosts converge to different discrete solutions, as expected when they discretize
the same continuous law differently: the sweep thus separates a truncation
pathology that convergence removes from a discretization difference that it does
not.

This cuts two ways: convergence largely cures the amplification --- iterating
further or adopting the implicit realization removes it --- so the bound of
\S\ref{sec:bound} is not a substitute for convergence but targets the regime
where neither escape is available. Interactive position-based solvers run
schedules near $1{\times}8$--$2{\times}4$ (the one-iteration small-step
regime~\citep{macklin2019small}), well below the $K\!\ge\!24$ this scene needs:
on $18$ deployed cells (3 scenes $\times$ 3 hosts, relaxation $0.7$) the
position-based host violates \eqref{eq:invariant} in all six of its cells (worst
$R=2282$, on just $8$ row evaluations) while the others match the sweep ($1/6$,
$0/6$).

\paragraph*{Condensing the shared rows is not the fix.} What converges the row
is the iteration budget, not how the shared support rows are scheduled: replacing
the serial per-row support projection with a joint block condensation of the
active rows (modal weight, implicit-midpoint restoring step, budget and warm
start held fixed; Fig.~\ref{fig:kconv}(c)) does \emph{not} remove the injection. It is comparable at the starved $4{\times}1$ corner but markedly
worse at every higher budget where the serial path holds ($R=12.5$ and $66.5$ at
$32{\times}1$ on shelf and ledge, against serial's $0.30$ and $0.09$). Reproduced
over two scenes and four budgets, it is a causal probe --- a different, worse
convergence path (diagonal rigid-body block approximation) --- not a cure.

\paragraph*{Not a knife-edge.} The catastrophic cells survive a predefined local
neighborhood. For each worst cell, the equal-row pair and the guardrail cell we
run $16$ paired deterministic perturbations --- $12$ physical (drop height
$\pm1$--$2\%$, normal speed, contact offset $\pm1.5$~mm, tilt) and $4$
contact-row-order permutations, kept as separate cohorts --- and every injecting
cell overdraws in all $16$, the sign never flipping, with a magnitude spread
under one order of magnitude ($\log_{10}$ range $0.31$--$0.70$); the
$4.4\times10^{7}$~J worst case is the maximum of a $2.2$--$4.5\times10^{7}$~J
band. The equal-row inversion ($32{\times}1$ holds, $4{\times}8$ injects, all
$16$) and the scene dependence (never injecting on the table) survive too. Mode
truncation localizes but does not remove it: excluding the stiff cluster cuts the
shelf $4{\times}1$ ratio $6333\to22.1$ ($584$~J still overdrawn) and $6$ of $8$
injecting cells still overdraw (worst ledge $+1.24\times10^{6}$~J), so
band-limiting the co-solved basis is not sufficient.

% =====================================================================
\section{A last-resort guardrail}
\label{sec:bound}
% =====================================================================
When a fixed host cannot converge the row and neither the implicit realization
nor more iterations are available, a deliberately minimal fail-safe holds
\eqref{eq:invariant} regardless of the contact solve: it credits a reservoir from
the measured supply and, when the realized modal state would overdraw it,
projects that state back inside.

\paragraph*{Enforcement.} A reservoir $B$ accumulates the supply and is debited
by realized storage. Both happen \emph{after} the contact solve, within the
same substep: $\dErig$ is not observable until the velocity solve
has finalized the rigid velocities, so the substep credits
$B \leftarrow B + \eta\max(\dErig,0)$ at that point, tests the realized modal
energy against it, and only then debits
$B \leftarrow \max(B - \max(\Delta\Emod,0),\,0)$. If
the realized modal energy would overdraw $B$, the state is projected onto the
admissible set by a single scalar,
\begin{equation}
(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) \;\leftarrow\; \gamma\,(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}),
\qquad
\gamma \;=\; \min\!\left(1,\;
  \sqrt{\frac{\Emod^{-} + B}{\Emod^{+}}}\right),
\label{eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
with $\Emod^{\mp}$ the modal energy before and after the solve. Each substep runs
identically in all three hosts: snapshot $E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{-},\Emod^{-}$;
predict and run the contact solve; form $\dErig$ (\eqref{eq:derig}, post-solve)
and credit $\eta\max(\dErig,0)$ to $B$ in the \emph{same} substep; if
$\Emod^{+}>\Emod^{-}+B$, scale the state by $\gamma$; debit $B$ --- contact is
\textbf{not} re-solved. The form \eqref{eq:gamma} is closed because $\Emod$ is
quadratic: scaling $\mathbf{q}$ and $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ together scales both terms
by $\gamma^2$, so it bounds total energy, not velocity alone, and is inert
whenever the solve is within budget ($\gamma{=}1$, bit-identical trajectories).

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:guarantee}
For any $\eta\in(0,1]$ and any host, the loop maintains $B\ge0$ and guarantees
\eqref{eq:invariant} unconditionally, assuming nothing about the contact solve,
up to an accounting tolerance $n\epsilon$ over $n$ substeps ($\epsilon$ the
per-test tolerance, $10^{-12}$~J).
\end{proposition}

\noindent\emph{Proof sketch.} Carry two invariants over substeps, with
$c_k=\eta\max(\dErig^{\,k},0)$: $B_k\ge0$ and
$(\Emod^{k}-\Emod^{0})+B_k\le\sum_{j\le k}c_j$ (both hold at $k{=}0$). Crediting
$c_k$ \emph{before} the test caps realized storage at $\Emod^{-}+B_{k-1}+c_k$
(as $\Emod$ is quadratic), so $\Delta\Emod\le B_{k-1}+c_k$; the debit keeps
$B_k\ge0$, and both invariants follow by induction. Since $B_n\ge0$ this is
\eqref{eq:invariant} itself, not a relaxation --- the same-substep credit
absorbs the granularity term a naive telescoping would leave.

\paragraph*{The governor holds.} Turned on, all $72$ sweep executions ($60$
distinct configurations, the implicit host's relaxation pairs bit-identical) and
the $18$ deployed cells of \S\ref{sec:kconv} satisfy \eqref{eq:invariant} --- $90$
governed cells at the roundoff floor (worst margin $1.1\times10^{-13}$~J). The
worst realized ratio falls to $1.22$ (position-based) and $0.87$
(augmented-Lagrangian); the projection is inert wherever the solve is already
within budget --- every implicit cell, and $16{\times}4$ up on the position-based
host at relaxation $0.7$.

\subsection{The cost of enforcement}
\label{sec:validity}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\caption{Post-projection contact validity for the \emph{position-based} host at
starved budgets, relaxation $0.7$, per clamp-active substep. Gap violation is
measured immediately after the $\gamma$-scale; the corrective impulse is the
next substep's normal impulse against the unclamped steady-state median, a ratio
because the hosts' multipliers are different objects. The $4{\times}1$ cells
clamp on nearly every substep, so no steady state exists there (---).}
\label{tab:validity}
\begin{tabular}{llrrrr}
\toprule
scene & budget & clamped & gap viol.\ med / max [mm] & impulse & $\lambda$ var. \\
\midrule
shelf & $4{\times}1$ & 107/108 & 1.24 / \textbf{21.6} & ---          & --- \\
shelf & $8{\times}2$ & 171/216 & 0.21 / 6.43          & $3.68\times$ & $5.6\times$ \\
ledge & $4{\times}1$ & 97/108  & 0.08 / \textbf{21.2} & $1.03\times$ & $1.08\times$ \\
ledge & $8{\times}2$ & 178/216 & 0.07 / 4.08          & $8.92\times$ & $62\times$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph*{Accuracy.} Bounding the energy is useful only if the bounded solution
improves on the unbounded one. At a moderate injecting cell (shelf, $8{\times}2$,
relaxation $0.7$) peak modal energy is $1555.6$~J ungoverned and $29.56$~J
governed against the implicit reference's $7.92$~J: the energy error falls
$196{\times}\to3.7{\times}$, and $189{\times}\to3.6{\times}$ against the XPBD
self-reference, so it does not depend on the reference. The trajectory, however,
degrades --- $\|d-d^{\text{ref}}\|_\infty$ goes from $6.5$~mm ($33\%$ of the
reference peak) to $14.2$~mm ($71\%$): the governor is a safety envelope, not an
accuracy device. At the deployed $1{\times}8$ cell energy gives
$2823{\times}\to3.7{\times}$ and the trajectory improves ($108\to96\%$ of
reference peak), though $96\%$ is still not faithful.

This is why a $196\times$ energy error coexists with a peak deflection only
$1.2\times$ too large: $99.6\%$ of the excess sits in the shelf's stiff mode
cluster above $20$~kHz (${\sim}200\times$ the substep rate), which a single
scalar cannot separate from the legitimate low-frequency sag --- $\gamma$ removes
the \emph{amount} but not the character ($99.6\to97.7\%$ above the cut), scaling
the sag ($24.1\to5.9$~mm against $20.0$) down with the noise. The first-line
remedy is band-limiting the basis, not a scalar.

\paragraph*{Contact validity.}
Since $\gamma<1$ shrinks the sag $\mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}$,
\eqref{eq:gamma} lifts the support \emph{into} the resting body without
re-solving contact. Table~\ref{tab:validity} quantifies the consequence,
instrumented by wrappers that leave the solve unperturbed (clamp counts
reproduce the independent sweep exactly).

Median post-projection penetration is $0.07$--$1.24$~mm, but the worst case
reaches $21.6$~mm, a $3.1$--$12.5\times$ increase over its pre-scale value ---
$72\%$ of the $30$~mm board thickness, and $1.05$--$1.08\times$ the board's peak
dynamic deflection: a visible interpenetration where the projection is most
load-bearing. Contact recovers on the next substep, but at a normal impulse up to
$8.9\times$ the steady-state value and multiplier variance up to $62\times$
higher; rigid momentum is unchanged (exactly zero, verified), since
\eqref{eq:gamma} writes only modal state. On the augmented-Lagrangian host the
projection is an order of magnitude gentler --- at its one materially-overdrawing
cell ($+6.7$~J) it opens $1.8$~mm against $21.6$, a single clamped substep, no
measurable corrective impulse (full rows, and a decision table over these
options, in the supplement).

% =====================================================================
\section{Fidelity and runtime}
% =====================================================================
\subsection{The reduced response against a full-FEM reference}
\label{sec:gt}
Modes are worth using only if the reduced response is faithful. Against an
unreduced FEM solve on the \emph{same} discrete operator (so discretization bias
cancels), the reduced ledge response tracks the reference: the peak-deflection
ratio rises $0.38\to0.54\to0.79\to0.88$ as $h$ refines $1/120\to1/960$ (the
residual ${\sim}10\%$ is $k{=}24$ truncation, not coupling error), the ring
frequency agrees to $0.4\%$ ($78.0$ vs $78.3$~Hz), and the far-field falloff
tracks at Spearman $\rho=0.89$ with no fitted attenuation.

\subsection{Runtime cost}
\label{sec:cost}
On the CPU host the ledger adds $0.23$--$0.41$~ms at $16{\times}4$ ---
$0.9$--$3.4\%$ on an $11$--$126$~ms baseline (the table scene's cost sits below
its run-to-run variance, so we report the percentage). It is larger where the
budget is tight: at the deployed $1{\times}8$/$2{\times}4$ schedules the same
${\sim}0.3$--$2.2$~ms is $6.6$--$34.3\%$. We make no unqualified real-time claim;
an \emph{enforced} device-resident $\gamma$ does not exist here
(\S\ref{sec:limits}).

% =====================================================================
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
% =====================================================================
\textbf{Stability is not accuracy.} Where the projection is load-bearing it
opens contact violations up to $21.6$~mm and moves the trajectory \emph{away}
from the implicit reference even as it moves the energy toward it
(\S\ref{sec:validity}): bounded, not faithful. Its honest use is a safety
envelope for budgets that would otherwise diverge; convergence is the better
remedy wherever affordable. A mechanism scaling deviations about the
quasi-static equilibrium rather than the whole state, preserving the
load-bearing sag, is unbuilt.

\textbf{Scope of the row.} The coupling is normal-only --- friction stays
body-local, so scraping and rolling transfer lie outside it --- and the
position-level form fixes $e{=}0$. The bound governs modal storage only, not
energy created spuriously in rigid DOFs: in the impulse realization, box--box
rows rectify a support ring into net rigid motion, to which the ledger is blind
by design.

\textbf{Supply and coverage.} The supply is a \emph{gross} sum, so energy
returned to the rigid bodies and re-dissipated is credited twice; we bound the
exposure by the opposite channel $\sum_k\max(-\dErig^{\,k},0)$ as a fraction of
supply --- $3$--$32\%$ (position-based), $0.4$--$27\%$ (implicit), $102$--$118\%$
on the augmented-Lagrangian host (whose rigid subsystem gains more than it loses
every cell, the box--box effect above) --- all above the ${\lesssim}1\%$
expected, and partition-dependent, so the budget belongs to the schedule as well
as the scene. Enforcement is host-side and single-machine (CPU float64); a
device-resident governor and a \emph{governed}-path FEM validation remain future
work. Three formulations, one implementation of each; three scenes, one contact
regime --- the augmented-Lagrangian host still overdraws in $3/24$ cells (up to
$6.7$~J), so any claim that descent-class solvers are passive here is empirical
about this sweep, not a theorem.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================
For a developer who has already chosen a fixed-budget XPBD rigid-body host and
wants low-cost vibration on a stiff prop, the decision is ordered, not XPBD
versus another solver. First pick the representation: full-space XPBD for large,
local or nonlinear deformation, a compact modal state for stiff,
small-displacement ringing. If the contact architecture is still open, the tested
stiffness-aware implicit realization is the cleanest control we observed (it
never overdraws), implementation-specific and not a solver-class theorem. If the
XPBD host is fixed, do not tune blindly: the direct two-way modal row overdraws
its measured supply by up to $4.4\times10^{7}$~J at a few local iterations, and
neither more substeps at equal row cost, nor warm-starting, nor condensing the
shared support rows into one block removes it (\S\ref{sec:kconv}); converging the
row with iterations does, so spend the budget there and verify the basis. Only
when a fixed host still cannot converge does the cumulative modal-storage bound
earn its place --- it holds in all $90$ measured cells but opens up to $21.6$~mm
of penetration, so it is containment, not corrected contact. A low-dimensional
modal extension is cheap in state size; it is not automatically easy for a
truncated local contact solve.
